newsitem.title: ALBANIA: IMF vows to help Albania firm up economy.
newsitem.headline: IMF vows to help Albania firm up economy.

text.p: TIRANA, July 30 (Reuter) The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has promised to help Albania's new government stabilize the shattered economy and deal with a pyramid savings scandal that toppled its predecessor, the government said on Wednesday.

The IMF's acting managing director Shigemitsu Sugisaki told Socialist Prime Minister Fatos Nano his organisation expected the centre-left government to take decisive action in implementing strong policies.

"The emergence of a government with a clear mandate and the ability to formulate and implement strong policies is vital for Albania's macro-economic reconstruction following the extraordinary crisis," Sugisaki said in a letter made available to Reuters.
"Please rest assured that the IMF remains eager and willing to help Albania," it continued.

The collapse of so-called pyramid schemes earlier this year sparked months of violence in Europe's poorest nation and led to the ousting of the right-leaning Democratic Party government and the resignation of former president Sali Berisha.
Nano, a 44-year-old economist, painted a bleak picture of Albania's economy as he presented the government's programme and warned of tough times ahead.
He pledged to halt further erosion of gross domestic product and soaring inflation, which is expected to reach up to 50 percent by the end of 1997.

Sugisaki said the Washington-based IMF was looking forward to sending a full mission to Tirana around mid-August "to initiate discussions on possible financial assistance that we could offer in support of a strong economic programme".
He added that the programe would require decisive action to promote macroeconomic stabilisation, deal effectively with pyramid schemes, and initiate structural reforms.
"And the IMF is fully prepared to advise your government in these areas," Sugisaki added.
He did not say when an agreement might be reached.
Finance Minister Arben Malaj has told parliament the government hoped to sign either a one-year standby agreement or a three-year accord with the IMF by the end of 1997.
He urged the new Socialist-dominated parliament to approve all the necessary fiscal elements for a much-needed deal, saying: "Everything will be conditional on the steps we take."
Since February large swathes of the country have been outside government control, meaning the authorities have been unable to collect some customs duties and taxes.
